title: Are festivals worth what they cost a town?

turns.speaker: Jules
turns.text: The festival brought eighty thousand people and the economic impact report says fourteen million.

turns.speaker: Emeka
turns.text: Those reports are almost always written by someone the festival paid.

turns.speaker: Shona
turns.text: And they tend to count every pound spent in town as new money, which it isn't. Some of it would have been spent anyway.

turns.speaker: Shona
turns.text: That, and leakage. If the food traders and the security firm all drive in from elsewhere, most of the money leaves with them on Monday.

turns.speaker: Emeka
turns.text: Meanwhile the residents get the road closures and the litter, and those are real costs that appear in nobody's total.

turns.speaker: Jules
turns.text: So is your position that it isn't worth it?

turns.speaker: Emeka
turns.text: No. My position is that the number is fiction and the case is better without it.

turns.speaker: Emeka
turns.text: People had a good weekend. The town looked alive. That's worth something and it doesn't need a spurious fourteen million attached.

turns.speaker: Shona
turns.text: Culture always ends up defending itself in an economic language it borrowed from somewhere else.

turns.speaker: Jules
turns.text: Because the council committee asks for a return on investment, not for a description of joy.

turns.speaker: Shona
turns.text: What does hold up is the year-round effect. Places with a strong festival tend to keep venues, technicians, suppliers.

turns.speaker: Emeka
turns.text: That I'd fund. The infrastructure rather than the weekend.

points: A festival claims fourteen million in economic impact from eighty thousand visitors.
Emeka notes such reports are usually commissioned by the festival itself.
Shona identifies displacement, where spending would have occurred anyway, and leakage, where external traders take money away afterwards.
Residents bear uncounted costs such as road closures and litter.
Emeka argues the figure is fiction and the cultural case is stronger without it, though councils demand economic justification.
Shona notes the durable benefit is year-round infrastructure, venues, technicians and suppliers, which Emeka would fund rather than the event.
